rv.q: Stunningly funny and utterly charming, Holden is enchanting.
As the West End reopens, the pick of the young crop is Jack Holden’s self-performed debut about life on London’s gay scene in the 1980s.
Cruise is a meaty, gloriously theatrical writing debut.
Cruise has more texture, variety and zip than most monologues and features some great music, but also longueurs and mawkish moments.
Holden performs with candour and excitement.
It’s a joyous, funny, moving piece and I urge you to see it.
Holden is incredible, never missing a beat or a note in the 90 minutes he spends on stage.
Its communal compassion is a terrific way to return to the stalls, a validation of all theatre can do.
Jack Holden’s “Cruise” confounds expectations by being an exultant embodiment of high-energy life.
Cruise pulses with a hedonistic abandon of its own only to emerge out the other side, Jack an auditor who is newly empowered by wisdom and compassion, too.
Holden is a remarkable tour de force in this witty and absorbing production.
Many twists of fate have given us one of the most incredible and must-see pieces of theatre to come to London for a long time.
Cruise is an important play for many people, for many reasons, but above all, it is a stunning piece of theatre with a lot of heart.

cn.t: Critics praise Holden's vibrant one-man show about gay life during the 1980s AIDS crisis as heartfelt and powerfully performed, though some note occasional longueurs. A moving, life-affirming West End reopening.
